question: Where does the take-off end, for performance purposes?
explanation: The take-off runs from the brake release point to the point where the aeroplane reaches a defined height, the screen height.

question: What is the take-off screen height for a Class A aeroplane?
explanation: The take-off screen height is 35 ft for Class A aeroplanes and 50 ft for Class B aeroplanes.

question: What is the take-off screen height for a Class B aeroplane?
explanation: Class B aeroplanes use a 50 ft take-off screen; Class A use 35 ft.

question: Which statement about a clearway is correct?

options.text: It is marked with yellow chevrons
It can be used to stop after a rejected take-off
It is an obstacle-free area, not a surface
It is a paved surface beyond the runway end, for stopping

explanation: Clearways are not physical structures; they are an area of defined width and length free of obstacles, used for the airborne part of the take-off.

question: Which statement about a stopway is correct?

options.text: It is a weaker paved surface used only for a rejected take-off
It is as strong as the runway and used for normal take-offs
It is an obstacle-free area that need not be paved
It may be used for landing in normal operations

explanation: Stopways are physical, usually paved surfaces, but are not as strong as the runway, so they are used only to stop after a rejected take-off.

question: How is a stopway marked?
explanation: Stopways are identified by large yellow chevrons at the runway ends.

question: How many of the four principal aerodrome distances apply to the take-off?
explanation: TORA, TODA and ASDA apply to the take-off; the fourth, LDA, applies to landing.

question: At most aerodromes, what is the take-off run available?

options.text: The runway length plus the clearway
The runway length plus the stopway at the far end

explanation: The TORA is usually the runway length from threshold to threshold.

question: A runway has no clearway. What is its TODA?
explanation: TODA = TORA + clearway, so with no clearway TODA equals TORA.

question: A runway has no stopway. What is its ASDA?
explanation: ASDA = TORA + stopway, so with no stopway ASDA equals TORA.

question: TORA 2 000 m, stopway 200 m, clearway 400 m. What are the ASDA and TODA?
explanation: ASDA = 2 000 + 200 = 2 200 m; TODA = 2 000 + 400 = 2 400 m. The clearway is within the half-TORA limit.

question: Which two parts make up the take-off distance?

options.text: The taxi distance and the ground run
The ground run and the stopping distance
The ground run and the airborne part
The airborne distance and the climb up to 1 500 ft above the runway

explanation: The take-off distance (TOD) is the ground roll from brake release plus the airborne distance to the screen height.

question: What is VLOF?

options.text: The speed at which the nose wheel lifts off the runway
The speed at which it becomes airborne
The speed at the screen height
The speed at which rotation begins

explanation: At VR the pilot starts to raise the nose; VLOF is the speed at which the aeroplane lifts off (the main wheels leave the ground).

question: What changes the calculated (gross) take-off distance into a net take-off distance?

options.text: Subtracting the airborne part of the distance

explanation: The calculated distance is the gross take-off distance; applying the regulations' safety factors gives the net take-off distance.

question: Which formula shows the distance needed to reach a speed V with a constant acceleration a?
explanation: s = V² ÷ 2a, with acceleration a = (thrust − drag) ÷ mass. Distance depends on the speed to be reached and the acceleration.

question: If the speed that must be reached is doubled, with the same acceleration, by what factor does the distance change?
explanation: Distance is proportional to V², so doubling the speed multiplies the distance by four.

question: The required ground speed at lift-off rises by 10% with the same acceleration. About how much does the ground run increase?
explanation: Distance ∝ V², so 1.1² = 1.21, an increase of about 21%.

question: For a jet engine, what is net thrust?

options.text: Gross thrust minus intake momentum drag
Thrust at full throttle minus idle thrust
Thrust per unit of fuel flow

explanation: Net thrust = gross thrust − intake momentum drag. Intake momentum drag rises with speed, so net thrust falls during the take-off run.

question: How does jet engine net thrust vary during the take-off run?

options.text: It falls to half by lift-off
It increases steadily as speed increases
It decreases slightly as speed increases

explanation: At take-off speeds the ram effect is too small to offset intake momentum drag, so thrust decreases a little. Graphs often treat it as constant for simplicity.

question: What does it mean that a jet engine is "flat rated"?

options.text: Its thrust is the same at every altitude
Its thrust is capped below a set temperature
It produces no thrust at all above a certain temperature
Its thrust rises steadily as temperature falls

explanation: A flat-rated engine is limited to a maximum thrust even though it could produce more at low temperatures, to protect the compressor from excessive pressures.

question: Below the flat-rating temperature (typically about ISA + 15°C), how does temperature affect take-off thrust?

options.text: It has no effect on thrust

explanation: Below the flat-rating cut-off, thrust is held at the rated maximum and does not increase as temperature falls.

question: Why is a jet engine flat rated?

options.text: To keep the turbine temperature constant
To protect the compressor at low temperatures
To save fuel at high temperatures

explanation: At low temperatures the engine could make so much thrust that internal pressures would exceed their limits, so thrust is capped.

question: How does the thrust of a propeller aeroplane vary during the take-off run?

options.text: It decreases as forward speed increases
It increases until the governor operates, then falls to zero
It increases as forward speed increases

explanation: Blade angle of attack falls as forward speed rises, so propeller thrust decreases with speed. A constant-speed propeller reduces the rate of decrease once the governor acts.

question: For a fixed-pitch propeller, why does thrust fall as forward speed increases?

options.text: The blade angle of attack falls
The engine rpm falls as the propeller unloads

explanation: For a fixed pitch, higher forward speed reduces the blade angle of attack and so the thrust.

question: How does a supercharged piston engine differ from an unsupercharged one with increasing altitude?

options.text: It gains power as altitude increases
It loses power faster than an unsupercharged engine does
It can maintain power at any altitude
It holds power up to full throttle height

explanation: An unsupercharged engine loses power as density falls; a supercharged engine can hold its power up to the full throttle height.

question: Which expression gives total drag during the ground run?
explanation: Total drag = aerodynamic drag plus wheel drag, where wheel drag is the friction coefficient μ times the load on the wheels (W − L).

question: How does wheel drag change during the take-off run?

options.text: It decreases as lift unloads the wheels

explanation: Wheel drag depends on the wheel load (W − L). As lift builds with speed the load falls, so wheel drag falls, reaching zero at lift-off.

question: How does induced drag change during the take-off?

options.text: It falls steadily during the take-off
It is zero throughout the ground run and climb

explanation: Angle of attack is roughly constant on the ground run, but rotation increases it greatly, so induced drag rises.

question: How does total drag change during the take-off run?

options.text: It increases, because aerodynamic drag rises faster than wheel drag falls
It falls to zero at lift-off
It decreases, because wheel drag falls faster than aerodynamic drag rises

explanation: The increase in parasite and induced drag outweighs the fall in wheel drag, so total drag increases.

question: During the take-off, what happens to the excess thrust and the acceleration?

options.text: Excess thrust increases but acceleration decreases

explanation: Thrust falls and drag rises, so the excess (T − D), and with it the acceleration, falls as the take-off proceeds.

question: Which speed appears in the take-off distance formula?
explanation: The distance depends on the true ground speed, so density (TAS for a given IAS) and wind (TGS for a given TAS) both matter.

question: Which requirement does the take-off safety speed meet?

options.text: It is the speed at which flaps are retracted
It is the speed for best lift-to-drag ratio
It has margins over stall and VMC, with climb
It is the highest speed at which the brakes can stop the aeroplane in time

explanation: The take-off safety speed must give a safe margin above the stall speed and minimum control speed and adequate climb, allowing for acceleration after lift-off.

question: How many separate effects does an increase in mass have that lengthen the take-off distance?
explanation: Greater mass reduces acceleration (inertia), increases wheel drag, raises the take-off safety speed and reduces the initial climb angle to the screen.

question: Why does increased mass increase wheel drag during the take-off run?

options.text: It increases the tyre pressure and rolling resistance
It increases the load on the wheels

explanation: Wheel friction depends on the load on the wheels, which rises with mass, so wheel drag rises and acceleration falls.

question: Which three factors determine air density?
explanation: Density depends on pressure, temperature and humidity. Lower pressure, higher temperature or higher humidity all reduce density.

question: How does low air density lengthen the take-off distance?

options.text: Higher wheel drag and a lower TAS
It has no effect on a turbine aeroplane
Less thrust, higher TAS, shallower climb
More thrust but a lower TAS for the same IAS at lift-off

explanation: Low density reduces thrust or power, increases the TAS needed for the same IAS, and reduces the initial climb angle, all lengthening the distance.

question: An aeroplane must reach a take-off safety speed of 120 kt TAS with a 20 kt headwind. What ground speed must it reach?
explanation: Ground speed = TAS − headwind = 120 − 20 = 100 kt, so less distance is needed. Applying the 50% rule for planning would give 110 kt.

question: How does a headwind affect the take-off?

options.text: It has no effect on the distance
It reduces the distance but makes the climb shallower
Shorter distance, steeper climb over the ground
It increases the distance but steepens the climb over the ground

explanation: A headwind reduces the ground speed needed and steepens the climb relative to the ground, both shortening the take-off distance.

question: What wind components must be assumed when calculating take-off distance?

options.text: No more than 50% of the headwind and no less than 150% of the tailwind
The full headwind and the full tailwind
No more than 150% of the headwind and no less than 50% of the tailwind
No headwind at all and twice the tailwind

explanation: The regulations allow for variations in the reported wind by assuming at most 50% of a headwind and at least 150% of a tailwind. Most charts already include this.

question: The reported wind gives a 12 kt tailwind component. What component must be used for take-off planning (if the chart does not include it)?
explanation: At least 150% of the tailwind must be used: 1.5 × 12 = 18 kt.

question: A take-off chart has the wind factors built in. Which wind should be entered?
explanation: When the factors are included in the graph, the reported wind is entered and the chart applies the corrections itself.

question: The wind is a pure 90° crosswind. What wind component is used for the take-off distance?

options.text: 150% of the wind speed as a tailwind
50% of the wind speed as a headwind

explanation: A 90° crosswind has no headwind or tailwind component, so the distance is the zero-wind value.

question: How does an uphill runway slope affect the take-off?

options.text: A component of weight adds to the thrust, so the distance shortens
It has no effect on the distance
Weight opposes thrust, so the distance grows
It reduces the wheel drag, shortening the distance

explanation: On an upslope, W × sin(slope) acts backwards like extra drag (weight apparent drag), reducing acceleration and increasing the distance.

question: How is the weight component along a sloping runway found?

options.text: Weight ÷ sine of the slope angle
Weight × cosine of the slope angle
Weight × sine of the slope angle

explanation: The component of weight along the runway is W × sin θ. On a downslope it adds to thrust (weight apparent thrust); on an upslope it adds to drag.

question: How does runway contamination by slush or standing water affect the take-off run?

options.text: It reduces drag, shortening the distance
It adds drag up to the hydroplaning speed, lengthening the distance
It adds drag only above the hydroplaning speed, not below it
It has no effect until braking is needed

explanation: Contamination adds displacement and impingement drag, which rises with speed until the hydroplaning speed, after which it falls. Overall the take-off distance increases.

question: Why is the stopping distance after a rejected take-off much longer on a wet or icy runway?

options.text: The braking friction is much lower, so brake pressure must be reduced
The aeroplane accelerates faster on a wet runway
The engines produce more reverse thrust on a wet runway
The stopway cannot be used when wet

explanation: The braking friction coefficient is severely reduced, so brake pressure must be limited to prevent skidding, greatly increasing the stopping distance.

question: What is required of the airframe at the start of the take-off run?

options.text: It may carry light frost on the upper wing
It may carry snow if the anti-ice is on
It may carry ice up to 3 mm thick
It must be free of ice and snow

explanation: Take-off data assume an uncontaminated airframe, and the aeroplane must be free of ice and snow at the start of the take-off, since contamination adds weight and drag and reduces lift.

question: How does increasing the take-off flap angle affect the take-off distance?

options.text: It falls, then rises past an optimum
It has no effect on the distance

explanation: More flap raises CLMAX and lowers take-off speeds, but also adds drag. The distance falls up to an optimum flap setting and then rises again.

question: In hot and high conditions, why might a smaller flap setting allow a greater take-off mass?

options.text: It shortens the take-off distance available

explanation: Less flap means less drag and a better climb gradient, so the mass–altitude–temperature limit rises, even though more runway is used.

question: Close-in obstacles are not cleared with the flap setting that gives the shortest take-off distance. What might help, if runway is available?

options.text: Using a lower flap setting for a better climb gradient
Using a higher flap setting for a lower lift-off speed

explanation: A lower flap angle uses more of the TODA but may give a steep enough gradient to clear the obstacles.
